questions.hook: This patient is in shock—don’t mistake tamponade for acute coronary syndrome, okay?
questions.vignette: A 63-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea and chest discomfort after a recent viral illness. He appears anxious and is sitting upright. Vitals: BP 88/60 mmHg, HR 112/min, RR 26/min, SpO2 93% on room air, and he is afebrile. Exam shows elevated jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds. Bedside cardiac ultrasound demonstrates pericardial effusion with right-sided diastolic collapse. On pulse oximetry, the systolic blood pressure decreases by 18 mmHg during inspiration. ECG shows low voltage without ischemic changes; troponin is normal.
questions.short_vignette: Hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds, echo shows pericardial effusion with right diastolic collapse; systolic BP drops 18 mmHg on inspiration.
questions.stem: Which physical exam finding most directly supports the diagnosis of cardiac tamponade?

options.text: Systolic blood pressure decreases >10 mmHg with inspiration
options.why: In tamponade, increased intrapericardial pressure accentuates impaired right ventricular filling during inspiration, causing pulsus paradoxus.
options.would_make_right: Increase the inspiration-related systolic BP drop from 18 mmHg to 12 mmHg while keeping the pericardial effusion and right diastolic collapse.

options.text: New systolic murmur that radiates to the carotids
options.why: A carotid-radiating systolic murmur suggests aortic stenosis rather than pericardial effusion with impaired diastolic filling.
options.would_make_right: Replace the pericardial effusion and diastolic collapse on ultrasound with aortic valve calcification and a loud crescendo-decrescendo murmur.

options.text: ST-segment elevations in contiguous leads with elevated troponin
options.why: ST-elevation and troponin elevation indicate acute MI, not tamponade physiology.
options.would_make_right: Change the ECG to show ST elevations and add elevated troponin while removing echo evidence of pericardial effusion.

options.text: Bilateral wheezing with prolonged expiration and normal jugular venous pressure
options.why: Wheezing and a normal JVP point toward obstructive lung disease rather than increased pericardial pressure.
options.would_make_right: Add diffuse wheezes, give normal JVP, and remove the ultrasound finding of pericardial effusion.

options.text: Focal neurologic deficits that progress over hours with fever
options.why: Progressive focal deficits with fever suggest a neurologic infectious/inflammatory process rather than a cardiopulmonary mechanical cause.
options.would_make_right: Replace cardiopulmonary findings with neurologic signs (eg, weakness, aphasia) and omit the echo/pressure changes.

questions.rule: Cardiac tamponade causes impaired ventricular filling that produces pulsus paradoxus during inspiration.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular Infections/Cardiac Tamponade and Pericardial Disease
American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association guidance on pericardial disease

questions.hook: “New fever after dental work—does endocarditis still require preexisting valve damage?”
questions.vignette: A 56-year-old man has 2 days of fever and malaise after dental cleaning. He reports increasing shortness of breath. On exam, temperature is 39.2 C (102.6 F), pulse 112/min, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg. A new holosystolic murmur is heard at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla. Labs show WBC 15,800/mm3 and C-reactive protein 12.5 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows no casts. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates a mitral valve vegetation. Which mechanism best explains why his risk was higher than in a young healthy adult?
questions.short_vignette: Older man develops fever after dental work. Echo shows mitral vegetation and new holosystolic murmur. What predisposition explains higher risk?
questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains why his risk was higher than in a young healthy adult?

options.text: Endothelial injury exposes platelets, enabling bacterial adherence
options.why: Infective endocarditis requires bacteria to adhere to damaged endocardium, where platelet-fibrin deposition creates a nidus for colonization. Predisposing valve lesions increase likelihood of this process after transient bacteremia.
options.would_make_right: Add a sentence that his echocardiogram shows chronic mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation before infection.

options.text: Impaired neutrophil chemotaxis allows bacteria to invade myocardium directly
options.why: Neutrophil chemotaxis defects are associated with recurrent bacterial infections but do not specifically describe the pathogenesis of endocardial vegetation formation on valve surfaces.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to document a congenital neutrophil adhesion/chemotaxis disorder and remove the new valve murmur.

options.text: Renal hypoperfusion causes bacterial growth in the bloodstream
options.why: Prerenal states predispose to acute kidney injury, not bacterial adherence on valves or vegetation formation. His urinalysis does not suggest a renal perfusion problem.
options.would_make_right: Replace CRP and echocardiography findings with low urine sodium and muddy brown casts, and remove evidence of valve vegetation.

options.text: Autoantibodies bind cardiolipin, causing sterile thrombi and emboli
options.why: Antiphospholipid syndrome causes thrombotic, sterile lesions rather than infectious vegetations with bacterial colonization after bacteremia.
options.would_make_right: Add positive antiphospholipid antibodies and remove the echo finding of vegetation.

options.text: Systemic viral infection reactivates dormant bacteria without bacteremia
options.why: Viral reactivation without bacteremia does not explain how bacteria reach and adhere to cardiac valves. Infective endocarditis classically follows transient bacteremia from procedures or infections.
options.would_make_right: Remove the dental trigger and instead describe chronic viral prodrome only, with no transient bacteremia.

questions.rule: Infective endocarditis forms when transient bacteremia seeds damaged endocardium with platelet-fibrin thrombi.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular Infections
AHA/IDSA Infective Endocarditis guideline (pathogenesis overview)

questions.hook: He feels arm BP is high—don’t assume aortic stenosis explains upper-body hypertension.
questions.key_finding: Upper BP high; lower BP low
questions.vignette: A 14-year-old boy presents with headaches and leg fatigue when running. His mother reports noticing decreased exercise tolerance over several months. Vitals show BP 165/90 mmHg in the right arm and 110/65 mmHg in the right leg; heart rate is 92/min. Cardiac exam reveals a systolic murmur best heard over the left infraclavicular area. An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. A chest X-ray demonstrates rib notching. No fever or murmur timing suggesting infection is present.
questions.short_vignette: Arm BP 165/90, leg BP 110/65; systolic murmur; LVH; rib notching—upper hypertension with lower hypotension.
questions.stem: Which finding best supports coarctation of the aorta over a valvular problem?

options.text: Higher systolic BP in arms than legs
options.why: Coarctation causes fixed narrowing of the aorta distal to the branch vessels to the upper extremities, producing arm hypertension and leg hypotension. This pattern localizes the problem to the aorta rather than the aortic valve.
options.would_make_right: Keep arm BP 165/90 and leg BP 110/65; mention explicit arm-minus-leg systolic gradient.

options.text: Ejection murmur with bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure
options.why: Aortic stenosis typically produces a late-peaking systolic murmur with diminished/slow-rising pulses, not bounding pulses with wide pulse pressure. The vignette’s arm–leg BP difference argues against a purely valvular explanation.
options.would_make_right: Change vitals to show equal arm and leg systolic BP and describe slow-rising pulses.

options.text: Low-grade fever and splinter hemorrhages on exam
options.why: Those findings suggest infective endocarditis rather than coarctation. The vignette’s primary clue is differential BP between arms and legs.
options.would_make_right: Add fever, positive blood cultures, and new/changed murmur; remove arm–leg BP discrepancy.

options.text: Bilateral decreased arm pulses with equal arm and leg pressures
options.why: This would not fit coarctation because coarctation primarily affects distal aortic flow to the lower extremities, not both arms equally. Equal arm and leg pressures would undermine the vascular gradient.
options.would_make_right: Change vitals to equal systolic BP in arms and legs and document diminished pulses in both arms.

options.text: Markedly decreased oxygen saturation with diffuse lung crackles
options.why: Respiratory findings suggest pulmonary pathology, not aortic narrowing. Coarctation explains systemic hypertension in the upper body with reduced perfusion to the legs.
options.would_make_right: Replace the cardiovascular exam with severe hypoxemia, crackles, and remove rib notching/arm–leg BP data.

questions.rule: In coarctation, compare extremities: upper-body hypertension with lower-body hypotension localizes aortic narrowing.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular System (Congenital Heart Disease/Hypertension)
AHA/ACC congenital heart disease review (physical exam: arm-leg BP gradient)

questions.hook: Listen closely: which maneuver causes an increase in the murmur for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
questions.vignette: A 26-year-old man reports exertional lightheadedness and chest discomfort. Exam shows a harsh systolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border that becomes louder with standing. Blood pressure is 132/70 mmHg supine and 104/66 mmHg standing; heart rate rises from 76 to 98/min. ECG shows LV hypertrophy with deep, narrow Q waves. An echocardiogram demonstrates asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction. Which bedside maneuver would most increase the murmur’s intensity?
questions.short_vignette: Young man has HCM with LV outflow obstruction; standing lowers BP and worsens murmur. Which maneuver increases murmur most?
questions.stem: Which bedside maneuver would most increase the systolic murmur intensity in this patient?

options.text: Squatting
options.why: Squatting increases venous return (increases preload), which reduces dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction in HCM. The murmur should decrease, not increase.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to say the murmur decreases with standing (suggesting increased preload worsens obstruction), and add that squatting makes it louder.

options.text: Passive leg raise
options.why: Passive leg raise increases preload and thereby decreases the degree of dynamic outflow obstruction. In HCM, increased preload typically makes the murmur softer.
options.would_make_right: Modify the vignette so that passive leg raise decreases BP and increases murmur, indicating the opposite preload effect.

options.text: Standing quickly (decreased preload)
options.why: HCM causes dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction that worsens when preload decreases. This increases the murmur intensity, consistent with the patient’s standing-related worsening.
options.would_make_right: Provide vitals demonstrating that standing lowers BP and loudness parallels worsening LV obstruction on repeat echo.

options.text: Inhalation of a bronchodilator causing tachycardia
options.why: Tachycardia can affect murmur timing/diastolic filling, but the key bedside determinant tested here is preload. This distractor targets a misconception that any tachycardia increases the murmur regardless of preload.
options.would_make_right: Alter the vignette to explicitly state the maneuver selectively decreases preload without changing volume status and then worsens the murmur.

options.text: Rapid isotonic fluid bolus (increased preload)
options.why: Increasing preload reduces dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction, so the systolic murmur intensity should decrease. This option flips the expected preload effect.
options.would_make_right: Add a statement that fluid administration decreases BP and paradoxically increases murmur; that would make this option correct.

questions.rule: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, decreased preload increases dynamic LV outflow obstruction and the systolic murmur.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular System
Dynamic LV outflow obstruction (HCM) preload maneuvers

questions.hook: “It’s just stable angina—same plaques, no rupture.” What is occurring in the culprit artery?
questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man with long-standing exertional chest discomfort arrives 1 hour after sudden-onset substernal pressure at rest. He is diaphoretic. Blood pressure is 98/62 mmHg, heart rate 112/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. ECG shows new ST-segment depression in leads V4–V6. High-sensitivity troponin I is elevated at 1.8 ng/mL (reference <0.04). He smokes and has hyperlipidemia. Coronary angiography demonstrates an irregular plaque with a superimposed intraluminal thrombus at the site of maximal stenosis. What process most directly explains the acute event?
questions.short_vignette: 62M sudden rest pain, hypotension, ST depression, troponin elevated; angiography shows irregular plaque with intraluminal thrombus.
questions.stem: Which pathologic event most directly triggers this acute coronary syndrome?

options.text: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed platelet-rich thrombus
options.why: Acute coronary syndromes are driven by disruption of an atherosclerotic plaque, exposing thrombogenic material. This promotes platelet activation and thrombus formation, causing partial or complete coronary occlusion.
options.would_make_right: Change angiography wording to “fibrous cap rupture with overlying thrombus,” and keep troponin elevated and ST depression.

options.text: Progressive concentric plaque growth causing fixed, slowly worsening stenosis
options.why: Stable angina results from chronic, fixed obstruction due to gradual plaque progression. The vignette emphasizes sudden onset and thrombus formation, which are not features of purely stable stenosis.
options.would_make_right: Replace angiography finding with “smooth plaque without thrombus” and change presentation to exertional pain relieved by rest.

options.text: A chronic thrombus organization that gradually narrows the lumen over months
options.why: Organized chronic thrombus can contribute to stable obstruction, but the scenario shows acute symptoms within hours and an intraluminal thrombus over an irregular plaque. Timing and morphology point to plaque disruption rather than long-term organization.
options.would_make_right: Alter the vignette so symptoms evolve gradually over months, and angiography shows “organized mural thrombus with no acute thrombus.”

options.text: Coronary vasospasm without any plaque disruption or thrombosis
options.why: Vasospastic angina involves transient coronary artery constriction, typically without thrombus or plaque rupture. The angiography explicitly shows superimposed intraluminal thrombus.
options.would_make_right: Change angiography to “transient narrowing that resolves with vasodilator, no thrombus,” and remove troponin elevation.

options.text: Hemorrhage into the plaque with immediate inhibition of platelet aggregation
options.why: Intramural plaque hemorrhage can occur, but acute coronary syndromes still involve thrombosis and platelet activation. The vignette demonstrates an active thrombus, not inhibited platelet aggregation.
options.would_make_right: State that angiography shows plaque hemorrhage but also “no thrombus” and that platelet function markers indicate inhibited aggregation.

questions.rule: Acute coronary syndromes commonly occur from plaque disruption that exposes thrombogenic material, triggering platelet-rich thrombus.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular Pathology
ACC/AHA guideline summaries on Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.hook: He thinks his “fluid overload” is the only cause—what actually drives HFrEF symptoms?
questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man with known dilated cardiomyopathy presents with 3 weeks of worsening exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. He reports decreased urine output. Vitals are T 37.0°C, HR 104/min, BP 92/60 mmHg, RR 22/min, and SpO2 94% on room air. Exam shows elevated JVP and bibasilar crackles. Labs show Na 131 mEq/L, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, and BNP 980 pg/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals LVEF 25%. ECG shows sinus tachycardia.
questions.short_vignette: 62M with LVEF 25%, hypotension, hyponatremia, JVP, crackles—what pathway primarily causes the worsening symptoms?
questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains his progressive symptoms in HFrEF?

options.text: Baroreceptor-mediated renin release causing vasoconstriction via RAAS
options.why: Low effective arterial blood volume in HFrEF activates baroreceptors, increasing renin, angiotensin II, and aldosterone. Angiotensin II increases systemic vascular resistance, worsening afterload and symptoms.
options.would_make_right: Replace “decreased urine output” with “low effective arterial blood volume from reduced forward flow,” while keeping BP low and LVEF 25%.

options.text: Systemic vasodilation from excess nitric oxide leading to compensatory tachycardia only
options.why: In HFrEF, the dominant compensatory response is vasoconstriction (increased SVR) from RAAS activation, not primary nitric-oxide–mediated vasodilation. Tachycardia occurs, but the main driver is increased afterload and volume retention.
options.would_make_right: Change BP to markedly low with warm extremities and explicitly state chronic severe sepsis physiology; that would shift mechanisms away from typical HFrEF compensation.

options.text: Primary intrinsic kidney failure causing fluid retention independent of neurohormonal activation
options.why: He has mild renal dysfunction, but the key trigger is reduced perfusion (“effective arterial blood volume”) activating RAAS and sympathetic pathways. Primary intrinsic renal failure would be expected to present differently and not fit the described HFrEF mechanism.
options.would_make_right: Add urinalysis findings consistent with intrinsic renal disease (eg, muddy brown casts) and remove evidence of neurohormonal activation patterns.

options.text: Pulmonary arterial smooth muscle hypertrophy causing fixed outflow obstruction
options.why: Pulmonary arterial smooth muscle hypertrophy leads to pulmonary hypertension and right-sided strain patterns. The vignette centers on LV systolic failure with reduced LVEF and classic HFrEF compensation.
options.would_make_right: Include right-heart catheterization showing chronically elevated pulmonary vascular resistance with preserved LVEF.

options.text: A primary valvular lesion causing sudden left atrial pressure spikes
options.why: HFrEF due to reduced LVEF is primarily a myocardial pump problem with neurohormonal activation. Aortic or mitral valvular disorders would create different hemodynamics and exam/lab patterns.
options.would_make_right: Add echocardiographic evidence of severe valvular disease (eg, severe mitral regurgitation with preserved LVEF) and remove dilated cardiomyopathy context.

questions.rule: In HFrEF, reduced forward flow triggers baroreceptor-driven RAAS activation, increasing afterload and worsening symptoms.

ACC/AHA Heart Failure guideline (general mechanism: neurohormonal activation in HFrEF)

questions.hook: “If the PR interval gets longer, it must be a first-degree block, right?”
questions.vignette: A 67-year-old man presents with dizziness and near-syncope after feeling “weak all day.” Vitals show blood pressure 126/68 mmHg, pulse 38/min and regular. ECG demonstrates P waves at a rate of 60/min, but the QRS complexes occur at 38/min with no consistent relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. Labs show potassium 4.2 mEq/L and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. He has no chest pain. Which mechanism best explains his ECG pattern?
questions.short_vignette: ECG shows bradycardia with P waves independent from QRS rate—AV dissociation. What mechanism causes this rhythm?
questions.stem: What mechanism best explains the ECG pattern in this patient?

options.text: Failure of impulse conduction through the AV node
options.why: In complete heart block, impulses from atria cannot reliably traverse the AV node, so atrial and ventricular rhythms become independent (AV dissociation).
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette ECG description to explicitly note no consistent P-to-QRS relationship due to blocked AV-node conduction.

options.text: Prolonged PR interval from delayed AV nodal conduction without complete separation
options.why: First-degree AV block has all P waves followed by QRS complexes with a uniformly prolonged PR interval, not independent atrial and ventricular rates.
options.would_make_right: Alter the ECG finding so every P wave is followed by a QRS with a consistently prolonged PR interval.

options.text: Reentrant ventricular tachycardia causing irregularly timed QRS complexes
options.why: Ventricular tachycardia typically produces wide QRS complexes with a rate driven by ventricular reentry, not AV dissociation with independent P waves at a different fixed rate.
options.would_make_right: Replace the ECG description with sustained wide-complex tachycardia and no discrete independent atrial rhythm.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with variable AV nodal conduction to the ventricles
options.why: Atrial fibrillation produces no discrete P waves; QRS timing varies due to irregular AV nodal conduction, rather than clear AV dissociation with organized P waves.
options.would_make_right: Modify the ECG to show absent P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm.

options.text: Sinus bradycardia where each sinus impulse conducts normally to the ventricles
options.why: Sinus bradycardia preserves 1:1 AV conduction, so P waves and QRS complexes remain linked; it does not produce AV dissociation.
options.would_make_right: Change the ECG to show 1:1 relationship between P waves and QRS complexes despite a slow rate.

questions.rule: In complete heart block, atria and ventricles beat independently due to failure of AV conduction (AV dissociation).

questions.hook: This patient’s cough is over—now think immune complex GN, not ongoing bacterial infection.
questions.vignette: An 8-year-old boy presents 2 weeks after a sore throat that resolved without antibiotics. He now has periorbital swelling and cola-colored urine. Vitals are T 37.1 C, BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 98/min. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood with dysmorphic RBCs and red blood cell casts. Serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. Serum albumin is 3.0 g/dL. Complement studies show C3 is low at 45 mg/dL. Throat culture is negative. What is the most likely underlying mechanism of his kidney injury?
questions.short_vignette: Child develops cola urine and RBC casts 2 weeks after sore throat; UA shows dysmorphic RBCs; C3 low.
questions.stem: What mechanism best explains this child’s post-streptococcal kidney findings?

options.text: Immune complex deposition with complement activation
options.why: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction. Streptococcal antigens trigger immune complex deposition in glomeruli and consumption of complement, especially low C3.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to specify C3 low and dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts after a recent untreated pharyngitis.

options.text: Anti-GBM antibodies causing linear basement membrane injury
options.why: Anti-GBM disease causes rapidly progressive GN with linear staining and typically severe pulmonary-renal syndrome features. The classic post-infectious timing with low C3 points to immune complex disease instead.
options.would_make_right: Add hemoptysis and specify linear IgG deposition on immunofluorescence.

options.text: ANCA-mediated necrotizing GN with pauci-immune inflammation
options.why: ANCA-associated vasculitis is characterized by pauci-immune necrotizing GN and often has systemic vasculitic symptoms; complement levels are not typically low. Timing after pharyngitis with low C3 supports immune complexes.
options.would_make_right: Add constitutional symptoms and require a positive c-ANCA with pauci-immune findings.

options.text: Antibody-dependent cytotoxicity of podocytes by IgE
options.why: Podocyte injury in GN is not mediated by IgE cytotoxicity. IgE mechanisms more closely relate to immediate hypersensitivity conditions and do not explain low C3 and post-streptococcal timing.
options.would_make_right: Replace the post-infectious story with an acute allergic trigger and add elevated IgE with normal C3.

options.text: Steroid-responsive nephrotic syndrome from podocyte effacement
options.why: Nephrotic syndrome from podocyte effacement presents with heavy proteinuria and edema, not cola urine with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts. Low C3 suggests glomerulonephritis rather than primary nephrotic syndromes.
options.would_make_right: Change the urinalysis to show 4+ protein with bland urine sediment and remove RBC casts.

questions.rule: Post-streptococcal GN is a type III immune complex reaction with low C3 and glomerular bleeding.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Renal Pathology
Immunology: Hypersensitivity Reactions (Type III)

questions.hook: “His pulse is fast—so should we immediately cardiovert him?”
questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man arrives with palpitations and mild shortness of breath that started 2 hours ago. He has no chest pain and no history of heart failure. Vitals: BP 128/78 mm Hg, HR 138/min, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, afebrile. ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm without visible P waves. Labs show normal electrolytes. Transthoracic echo shows no new regional wall motion abnormalities. He is alert and has no signs of shock or acute heart failure. He asks whether to “shock” him now.
questions.short_vignette: 2-hour palpitations, stable vitals, ECG: irregularly irregular without P waves. No shock or acute heart failure—what next?
questions.stem: Which immediate management best addresses his atrial fibrillation?

options.text: Immediate synchronized cardioversion
options.why: Cardioversion is urgent for unstable patients (eg, hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema). This patient is hemodynamically stable with no acute heart failure signs.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to include BP 86/54 mm Hg and rales with hypoxemia consistent with acute pulmonary edema.

options.text: Immediate rate control with an AV nodal blocker
options.why: In stable atrial fibrillation, the immediate goal is ventricular rate control using AV nodal blockade (eg, beta-blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker).
options.would_make_right: Keep the patient stable as written but specify worsening tachycardia symptoms without hypotension; rate control remains best.

options.text: Start anticoagulation only after 48 hours of atrial fibrillation
options.why: Anticoagulation decisions depend on duration and stroke risk; it is not delayed in a stable patient solely until 48 hours in the way described. Early anticoagulation may be indicated depending on risk and timing.
options.would_make_right: Specify a planned rhythm-control strategy for known duration <48 hours and include a stated stroke-risk indication that necessitates immediate anticoagulation rather than deferral.

options.text: Administer adenosine to terminate the rhythm
options.why: Adenosine treats AV nodal–dependent SVT and can transiently slow AV conduction, but it does not reliably terminate atrial fibrillation.
options.would_make_right: Change the ECG description to narrow-complex regular tachycardia with retrograde P waves (paroxysmal SVT pattern).

options.text: Give thrombolytic therapy for presumed myocardial infarction
options.why: Atrial fibrillation can coexist with ischemia, but there is no chest pain, no ischemic ECG described, and vitals and labs do not support MI requiring thrombolysis.
options.would_make_right: Add ECG evidence of ST-elevation myocardial infarction and chest pain with rising troponins.

questions.rule: In hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation, first control ventricular rate with AV nodal blockade rather than immediate cardioversion.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular Pharmacology
ACC/AHA/ESC Atrial Fibrillation guideline (management of stable vs unstable patients)

questions.hook: They think it’s just SVT—ignore the pattern on ECG.
questions.vignette: A 19-year-old man presents with sudden palpitations and lightheadedness lasting 20 minutes. Vitals: HR 168/min, BP 112/70 mmHg, RR 16/min, O2 sat 99% on room air, afebrile. Physical exam shows no murmurs. An ECG during symptoms shows a short PR interval and an initial slurred upstroke of the QRS complex. He later reports a history of similar brief episodes. A subsequent ECG done between episodes shows the same short PR interval.
questions.short_vignette: 19M with episodic palpitations; ECG shows short PR and slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave). What diagnosis explains this?
questions.stem: Which ECG finding best supports Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome as the cause of his arrhythmia?

options.text: Short PR interval with delta wave
options.why: WPW is caused by an accessory pathway that allows early ventricular activation, producing a short PR interval and a slurred initial QRS complex (delta wave).
options.would_make_right: Include an ECG description of an initial slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) with a short PR interval, prompting the diagnosis of WPW.

options.text: Prolonged PR interval with dropped beats
options.why: This describes AV nodal conduction delay with intermittent block, consistent with AV block rather than pre-excitation from an accessory pathway.
options.would_make_right: Change the ECG to show progressively prolonged PR followed by nonconducted P waves (dropped QRS), making AV block the correct answer.

options.text: Fusiform ventricular ectopy with irregularly irregular rhythm
options.why: An irregularly irregular rhythm with no consistent P waves points to atrial fibrillation, not WPW.
options.would_make_right: Modify the ECG to show no discrete P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular response, making atrial fibrillation correct.

options.text: ST-segment elevations in contiguous leads with reciprocal depression
options.why: ST elevations with reciprocal depression indicate acute MI, which can cause palpitations but is not the ECG pattern of WPW pre-excitation.
options.would_make_right: Replace the ECG findings with ST-segment elevation in a coronary distribution plus reciprocal changes, making acute MI correct.

options.text: Widened QRS complexes with complete absence of P waves
options.why: This describes ventricular tachycardia/escape rhythm depending on context, not the characteristic pre-excitation pattern of WPW.
options.would_make_right: Change the ECG to show wide-complex tachycardia without visible P waves and a mechanism consistent with ventricular tachycardia.

questions.rule: In WPW, look for pre-excitation: short PR plus a delta wave (slurred, widened QRS onset).
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiology: Cardiac Arrhythmias
American Heart Association ACLS (arrhythmia ECG patterns)

questions.hook: Thinking this is myocardial ischemia, you miss the pleuritic positional chest pain pattern.
questions.key_finding: Sharp pain, worse supine, better leaning forward
questions.vignette: A 28-year-old man presents with sudden chest pain for 2 days after a viral illness. He describes it as sharp and worse when lying flat and with deep breaths; he feels better sitting forward. Vitals: T 38.3 C, HR 104/min, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air. ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevations with PR depression. Troponin is 0.6 ng/mL (upper limit 0.04). White blood cell count is 12,800/mm3. An echocardiogram shows no pericardial effusion.
questions.short_vignette: Young man post-viral: sharp chest pain worse lying down and deep breath; ECG diffuse ST elevation, PR depression, no effusion.
questions.stem: Which physical finding best supports acute pericarditis rather than myocardial ischemia?

options.text: Chest pain worsens when lying flat and improves leaning forward
options.why: Positional, pleuritic pain occurs because pericardial inflammation changes contact between inflamed layers with posture and respiration. Myocardial ischemia classically is exertional pressure not specifically positional.
options.would_make_right: State in the vignette that pain decreases when he sits up and leans forward, and worsens supine.

options.text: Chest pain is reliably triggered by exertion and relieved by rest within minutes
options.why: Exertional relief suggests stable angina/myocardial ischemia physiology. Acute pericarditis pain is instead affected by body position and breathing.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to state pain occurs with exertion and quickly resolves with rest, with no positional dependence.

options.text: Pain begins after sudden leg swelling and migratory shortness of breath
options.why: This suggests pulmonary embolism, where symptoms may be pleuritic and acute, but the hallmark pericardial positional improvement is not expected. The ECG pattern described also points away from PE.
options.would_make_right: Add preceding unilateral leg swelling and describe symptoms primarily with exertion and tachycardia, removing positional pain detail.

options.text: Pain improves with nitrates and is associated with focal ST depressions
options.why: Nitrate responsiveness and focal ST changes support myocardial ischemia rather than pericarditis. Pericarditis has diffuse ST elevation and PR depression, not isolated focal depression.
options.would_make_right: Modify ECG description to focal ST depressions and make the pain consistently nitrate-responsive regardless of posture.

options.text: Pain is painless unless palpated over a single rib region
options.why: Localized reproducible tenderness suggests musculoskeletal chest wall pain. Pericarditis pain is typically pleuritic and positional rather than limited to a single palpation site.
options.would_make_right: Replace the positional description with strictly focal tenderness to palpation over one intercostal space.

questions.rule: In acute pericarditis, inflammatory chest pain is pleuritic and positional—worse supine, better leaning forward.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiology/Pericarditis
2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases

questions.hook: A cyanotic infant—don't mistake it for a left-sided obstructive lesion.
questions.vignette: A 2-month-old infant is brought for progressive cyanosis during feeding. The mother reports episodes of sudden worsening after crying. Vitals: T 37.0°C, HR 160/min, RR 42/min, BP 72/40 mmHg, SpO2 78% on room air. Physical exam shows a systolic ejection murmur best heard at the left upper sternal border and delayed femoral pulses are absent. Chest radiograph shows an enlarged right ventricle with a boot-shaped cardiac silhouette. Echocardiography demonstrates right ventricular hypertrophy and an overriding aorta with a ventricular septal defect.
questions.short_vignette: Infant cyanosis with crying; boot-shaped heart and overriding aorta on echo—confirm Tetralogy of Fallot.
questions.stem: Which embryologic defect best explains this infant’s tetralogy of Fallot?

options.text: Failure of neural crest cell migration to the outflow tract
options.why: Tetralogy of Fallot results from abnormal development of the outflow tract due to disrupted neural crest contributions, leading to malalignment and the classic defects.
options.would_make_right: Change echo description to explicitly note malalignment of the outflow tract with anterior deviation of the infundibular septum.

options.text: Incomplete fusion of the septum primum causing an atrial septal defect
options.why: An atrial septal defect causes increased right-to-left or left-to-right shunting at the atrial level, not right ventricular outflow obstruction with overriding aorta.
options.would_make_right: Replace the echo findings with a secundum atrial septal defect and normal outflow tract anatomy.

options.text: Failure of ductus arteriosus closure leading to persistent pulmonary hypertension
options.why: A patent ductus arteriosus can contribute to pulmonary overcirculation and heart failure, but it does not produce the boot-shaped heart or overriding aorta with ventricular septal defect.
options.would_make_right: Include echocardiography showing a persistent ductus arteriosus connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta without a ventricular septal defect.

options.text: Abnormal development of endocardial cushions causing atrioventricular septal defects
options.why: Endocardial cushion defects primarily affect atrioventricular septation (often with mitral/tricuspid valve abnormalities), not the combination of VSD, pulmonary stenosis, and overriding aorta.
options.would_make_right: Change exam to show complete atrioventricular canal features (common AV valve) and remove pulmonary outflow obstruction findings.

options.text: Failure of left ventricular hypertrophy regression causing coarctation physiology
options.why: Coarctation of the aorta involves abnormal aortic development leading to diminished lower-extremity perfusion, not right-sided outflow obstruction and overriding aorta.
options.would_make_right: Add physical findings of differential upper versus lower extremity blood pressures and imaging showing aortic narrowing.

questions.rule: Tetralogy of Fallot is a malformation of outflow tract alignment—classically tied to neural crest dysfunction.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular Pathology (Congenital Heart Disease)
Goljan/robust congenital heart disease embryology summaries (neural crest and outflow tract development)

questions.hook: A cyanotic newborn can be misdiagnosed as pulmonary disease; ask what lesion causes parallel rather than series flow.
questions.key_finding: Two parallel circuits: mixed only via shunt
questions.vignette: A 2-day-old male newborn has persistent cyanosis since birth and poor feeding. Vitals: T 36.8°C, HR 160/min, RR 52/min, BP 62/38 mmHg. Pulse oximetry shows SpO2 78% on room air. Exam reveals a loud single S2; there is no wheezing. Chest radiograph shows increased pulmonary vascular markings and a narrow mediastinum. Echocardiography demonstrates the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle. What underlying physiology best explains why cyanosis is present immediately after birth?
questions.short_vignette: Day-2 cyanotic neonate, SpO2 78% RA, echo: aorta from RV, pulmonary artery from LV. What physiology explains early cyanosis?
questions.stem: In this newborn with transposition of the great arteries, what physiologic problem causes immediate cyanosis?

options.text: Systemic and pulmonary blood circulate in parallel, requiring a shunt for mixing
options.why: In transposition, the great arteries are switched, so the right ventricle sends deoxygenated blood to systemic circulation and the left ventricle sends oxygenated blood back to the lungs. Effective oxygen delivery depends on mixing via ASD/VSD/PDA.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette echocardiography statement to explicitly “great arteries switched, creating parallel systemic and pulmonary circuits,” while maintaining the same cyanosis and oxygen saturation.

options.text: Left ventricular outflow obstruction prevents forward flow to the lungs
options.why: That mechanism would reduce pulmonary blood flow, leading to poor lung perfusion rather than increased/normal pulmonary vascular markings. It would not explain aorta arising from the right ventricle.
options.would_make_right: Replace the echo findings with “subvalvular or valvular left-sided outflow obstruction” and remove the great-artery switching.

options.text: Pulmonary artery supplies systemic circulation due to ductal constriction
options.why: Ductal constriction can worsen cyanosis in some congenital lesions by reducing mixing through PDA, but it does not explain the anatomic swapping of the great arteries. The vignette’s echocardiogram directly identifies the cause.
options.would_make_right: Add anechoic statement that great arteries are normally connected, and specify “PDA closure leads to sudden cyanotic deterioration” without switching.

options.text: Complete separation of circulations eliminates any need for atrial mixing
options.why: Complete separation would cause profound hypoxemia if oxygenated blood cannot reach systemic circulation. Cyanosis immediately after birth indicates that mixing is inadequate.
options.would_make_right: Modify the vignette to show a large VSD/ASD with near-normal oxygen saturation from birth, contradicting isolated parallel-circulation without mixing.

options.text: Right ventricular failure reduces pulmonary blood flow after birth
options.why: Early pulmonary hypoperfusion would typically present with decreased pulmonary vascularity. In transposition, increased oxygenated blood recirculates to the lungs while deoxygenated blood goes systemically.
options.would_make_right: Change the chest radiograph description to “decreased pulmonary vascular markings” and provide echo evidence of primary right-sided cardiomyopathy instead of arterial switching.

questions.rule: In transposition of the great arteries, switched great vessels create parallel circulations, so survival depends on mixing through shunts.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular System (Congenital Heart Disease)
AHA/ACC congenital heart disease physiology overview

questions.hook: A patient’s troponins rise—what mechanism explains MI risk right now?
questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man presents with 45 minutes of substernal chest pressure radiating to his left arm. He has diabetes and a prior history of smoking. Vitals: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 104/min, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air. ECG shows new horizontal ST-segment depression in leads V4–V6. High-sensitivity troponin I is 0.8 ng/mL (reference <0.04). He reports the pain began at rest. Which immediate coronary event most likely triggered plaque instability?
questions.short_vignette: 62M chest pressure at rest; ECG shows ST depression; troponin I elevated. Which immediate event caused acute coronary syndrome?
questions.stem: Which immediate event most likely triggered plaque instability in this acute coronary syndrome?

options.text: Rupture of a vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed platelet-rich thrombus
options.why: In ACS, myocardial ischemia is commonly initiated by plaque disruption, exposing thrombogenic material. This leads to platelet activation/aggregation and an occlusive thrombus that decreases coronary blood flow.
options.would_make_right: Add an angiographic note of an occlusive thrombus at the culprit lesion.

options.text: Progressive calcific valve leaflet thickening leading to fixed outflow obstruction
options.why: This describes aortic stenosis, which causes chronic left ventricular outflow limitation and exertional syncope/angina rather than acute ECG changes with troponin rise.
options.would_make_right: Replace ECG with systolic murmur findings and remove troponin elevation.

options.text: Chronic pressure overload causing ventricular hypertrophy without acute coronary thrombosis
options.why: Chronic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can cause ischemia, but ACS in this vignette is characterized by acute ECG ischemic changes and troponin elevation from coronary flow-limiting thrombosis.
options.would_make_right: Change vignette to longstanding exertional symptoms with no new ST changes and normal troponin.

options.text: Embolization of septic material to coronary arteries from left-sided endocarditis
options.why: Infective endocarditis can cause coronary emboli, but ACS here is presented with classic ischemic ECG changes and no systemic infectious symptoms or endocarditis context.
options.would_make_right: Add fever, positive blood cultures, and a new murmur with splinter hemorrhages.

options.text: Primary failure of the myocardium to relax, causing pulmonary venous congestion
options.why: Impaired relaxation is a heart failure/diastolic dysfunction concept and does not specifically explain plaque instability with thrombus that produces ACS with troponin elevation.
options.would_make_right: Add orthopnea with rales and change ECG/troponin to show heart failure without ischemic pattern.

questions.rule: Acute coronary syndromes usually result from disrupted atherosclerotic plaque with thrombus formation causing abrupt coronary flow reduction.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiology: Acute Coronary Syndromes
ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Non–ST-Elevation Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.hook: “This child has a new murmur—does that mean the problem is aortic valve disease?”
questions.key_finding: Holosystolic murmur at left sternal border
questions.vignette: A 3-week-old male is brought for poor feeding and sweating during feeds. Vitals: HR 170/min, RR 44/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, SpO2 94% on room air. Exam shows a single loud, harsh murmur that is heard throughout systole along the left lower sternal border. Chest X-ray shows mild cardiomegaly and pulmonary vascular congestion. An echocardiogram demonstrates a defect in the interventricular septum with left-to-right shunting. Which lesion best explains the murmur timing and location?
questions.short_vignette: 3-week infant with tachypnea, sweating feeds, CXR congestion; holosystolic murmur left lower sternal border; echo shows septal defect with L→R shunt.
questions.stem: Which congenital lesion most directly causes a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border?

options.text: Ventricular septal defect from abnormal closure of the interventricular septum
options.why: A VSD creates a pressure gradient throughout systole, producing a holosystolic murmur. The typical auscultation site is the left lower sternal border.
options.would_make_right: Keep the septal defect with left-to-right shunting on echo and add that the murmur is loudest at the left lower sternal border.

options.text: Aortic stenosis causing an ejection murmur that peaks in late systole
options.why: Aortic stenosis produces an ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur focused at the right upper sternal border and classically peaks in late systole. The vignette describes holosystolic timing and left lower sternal border location.
options.would_make_right: Change the murmur to crescendo-decrescendo only during systole and move the maximal intensity to the right upper sternal border with echo showing aortic valve narrowing.

options.text: Mitral regurgitation with a holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla
options.why: Mitral regurgitation is holosystolic but is best heard at the apex and may radiate to the axilla. The echo in the vignette shows a septal defect rather than valve dysfunction.
options.would_make_right: Replace the echo finding with mitral valve prolapse/regurgitation and change exam to a murmur loudest at the apex radiating to the axilla.

options.text: Atrial septal defect causing an ejection-type murmur from pulmonary flow increase
options.why: ASD murmurs are typically associated with increased pulmonary blood flow and commonly include a systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, often described as ejection-type rather than holosystolic. The vignette’s key finding is septal dysfunction in the interventricular septum.
options.would_make_right: Change echo to an interatrial shunt (e.g., secundum ASD) and move the murmur intensity to the left upper sternal border.

options.text: Patent ductus arteriosus producing a continuous “machinery” murmur
options.why: PDA causes a continuous murmur because flow occurs throughout systole and diastole. The vignette specifically describes a murmur throughout systole only.
options.would_make_right: Alter the murmur description to continuous and add echo evidence of a ductal shunt between the aorta and pulmonary artery.

questions.rule: A holosystolic murmur suggests flow across a ventricular-level defect like VSD, typically loudest at the left lower sternal border.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular System (Congenital Heart Disease)
American Heart Association congenital heart disease auscultation principles

questions.hook: A clinician thinks low O2 saturation in a newborn always means pneumonia—what PDA sign confirms shunt physiology?
questions.vignette: A 2-day-old term male newborn develops poor feeding and mild tachypnea. He has an audible continuous “machinery” murmur best at the left infraclavicular area. Vitals: HR 168/min, RR 54/min, BP 68/35 mmHg. Pulse oximetry shows SpO2 90% on room air. Chest radiograph reveals cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings. An echocardiogram demonstrates a left-to-right shunt through a persistent ductus arteriosus.
questions.short_vignette: Term newborn, continuous machinery murmur, mild tachypnea, SpO2 90%, echo shows left-to-right ductal shunt.
questions.stem: Which auscultatory finding most specifically supports patent ductus arteriosus?

options.text: Continuous machinery murmur best at left infraclavicular area
options.why: PDA produces turbulent blood flow between the aorta and pulmonary artery throughout the cardiac cycle, classically described as a continuous “machinery” murmur. The left infraclavicular location matches typical auscultation.
options.would_make_right: Keep the vignette murmur described as continuous and ensure echo shows left-to-right ductal shunt; this makes the stated auscultation the definitive correlate.

options.text: Systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids
options.why: This pattern is classic for aortic stenosis due to narrowed outflow during systole. A PDA causes flow throughout both systole and diastole.
options.would_make_right: Change the echo to show valvular aortic stenosis with no ductal patency; then carotid radiation would become the best answer.

options.text: Holosystolic murmur that increases with Valsalva
options.why: Holosystolic murmurs that change with Valsalva suggest dynamic obstruction or mitral regurgitation physiology. PDA does not produce a Valsalva-dependent holosystolic murmur.
options.would_make_right: Alter the vignette to include echo evidence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or mitral regurgitation; then Valsalva-dependent holosystolic murmur could be correct.

options.text: Diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border
options.why: A diastolic decrescendo murmur is typical of aortic regurgitation from backflow during diastole only. PDA generates a continuous murmur spanning systole and diastole.
options.would_make_right: Replace the echocardiogram finding with aortic regurgitation and remove ductal shunt; then a diastolic decrescendo murmur would fit.

options.text: Ejection click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex
options.why: An ejection click with a murmur at the apex suggests mitral valve pathology. PDA is characterized by continuous machinery-like flow, not an ejection click at the apex.
options.would_make_right: Modify the vignette echo to show mitral valve prolapse; then the ejection click and late systolic murmur would become correct.

questions.rule: A patent ductus arteriosus causes a continuous machinery murmur because flow persists through both systole and diastole.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiology: Congenital Heart Disease
ACOG/AHA general pediatric cardiology auscultation principles
